title: Configuration Comparison Automation with Claude
tagline: Two platforms, one verified difference report, before the change window opens
audience: Enterprise IT and network operations teams, load balancer and ADC engineers, cloud migration and platform engineers, infrastructure automation leads
prerequisites: Working knowledge of load balancers or ADCs (F5, NetScaler, Radware or similar) and basic cloud networking
Comfort with the command line, REST APIs and JSON
Familiarity with Git; prior use of Claude or an AI coding assistant is helpful, not required
outcomes: Plan a configuration comparison for cloud-to-cloud, physical-to-cloud and cloud-to-physical migrations, including what must be proven and what cannot be compared

Collect running configuration from F5 (iControl REST and tmsh), Citrix NetScaler (NITRO API), Radware Alteon, other load balancers (Anaya LB), Cisco APIC and Terraform state with read-only credentials
Normalise every platform into one canonical Pydantic model with provenance and explicit unknowns
Use Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK and MCP servers so that Claude plans and explains while deterministic Python computes the diff
Generate severity-classified difference reports, Claude-written explanations and remediation steps grounded in the report
Gate every consequential action behind GitHub pull request review and a ServiceNow change record, with a full audit trail of prompts, tool calls and decisions

modules.title: Configuration comparison as a migration discipline
topics: The three directions: cloud-to-cloud, physical-to-cloud, cloud-to-physical, and what each must prove before cut-over
Why a raw text diff between an F5 and a NetScaler configuration is worthless; semantic objects versus syntax
Scoping the comparison: virtual servers, pools, monitors, persistence, SSL profiles, policies, routing and NAT
The course pattern: Claude plans, drafts and explains; deterministic code executes; a person approves; everything is logged
modules.lab: Take a sample physical F5 configuration and a hand-built cloud NetScaler configuration and write, by hand, the comparison plan and object checklist that the pipeline must later automate.
modules.deliverable: Comparison plan template and object checklist.

modules.title: Setting up Claude Code, the Agent SDK and MCP for the workflow
topics: Installing Claude Code and configuring a project with CLAUDE.md conventions for the comparison repository
Claude Agent SDK basics: sessions, tool definitions, structured JSON outputs and when to use the SDK instead of the interactive CLI
Building a minimal MCP server that exposes read-only collector tools (get_virtual_servers, get_pools) to Claude
Secrets handling: credentials in environment variables and vaults, never in prompts or repositories
modules.lab: Stand up the workbench, register the read-only MCP server, and have Claude list the virtual servers on the lab F5 through tool use without ever seeing a password.
modules.deliverable: Configured workbench with a working read-only MCP collector.

modules.title: Collecting configuration from every platform
topics: F5: iControl REST (/mgmt/tm/ltm) and tmsh list output; Citrix NetScaler: NITRO API config resources
Radware Alteon via Cyber Controller and CLI exports; other load balancers (Anaya LB) through CLI capture adapters
Cisco APIC REST API for fabric objects and Terraform state (terraform show -json) for cloud-side resources
Collector contract: idempotent, read-only, timestamped, raw payload retained as evidence
modules.lab: Write Python collectors for F5 iControl REST and NetScaler NITRO against the lab devices, then Radware Alteon CLI export and Cisco APIC REST collectors against recorded API fixtures, with Claude drafting the code and you reviewing every diff.
modules.deliverable: Collector library with raw evidence capture for four platform families (F5, NetScaler, Radware Alteon, Cisco APIC).

modules.title: Normalising into a canonical configuration model
topics: Designing the canonical Pydantic model: VirtualServer, Pool, Member, Monitor, Persistence, SSLProfile, Policy
Mapping tables per platform and the rule that unmapped fields are marked unknown, never dropped silently
Provenance on every field: source platform, object name, collection time, raw reference
Validation tests for round-tripping fixtures through the model
modules.lab: Build the normaliser for F5 and NetScaler, run both lab configurations through it, and inspect the unknowns list with Claude explaining each one.
modules.deliverable: Canonical model, mapping tables and normalisation test suite.

modules.title: Migration planning with Claude
topics: Prompting Claude with the source inventory and target platform capabilities to draft a migration plan as structured JSON
Required fields: object mapping, feature gap, dependency order, risk, confidence, owner, and citation to the inventory
Handling incomplete or contradictory inventories: the plan must say what cannot be mapped
Reviewing and versioning plans in Git as the first human checkpoint
modules.lab: Generate a physical-to-cloud plan for the lab inventory, then feed Claude a deliberately contradictory inventory and verify it flags the conflict instead of inventing a mapping.
modules.deliverable: Migration planning agent with JSON schema and review checklist.

modules.title: The deterministic diff engine
topics: Field-by-field comparison of canonical models in Python; ordering, set semantics and tolerated differences
Severity classification rules: blocking, warning, informational, and platform-specific exemptions
Machine-readable diff report (JSON) plus a human summary; the engine never calls a model
Unit tests with pytest, including seeded mismatches that must always be caught
modules.lab: Implement the diff engine, seed a hidden persistence timeout mismatch into the target configuration, and prove the test suite catches it.
modules.deliverable: Tested diff engine producing severity-classified JSON reports.

modules.title: Claude explains the differences
topics: Giving Claude the diff report through tool use (get_diff, get_object) rather than pasting whole configurations
Structured explanation output: what differs, why it matters for traffic, recommended remediation, confidence, citation to the diff line
Drift summaries for operations managers and remediation steps for engineers from the same report
Guarding against hallucinated objects: every referenced object must exist in the report
modules.lab: Build the explanation agent with the Agent SDK, run it on the day's diff report, and verify every statement traces to a report line.
modules.deliverable: Explanation agent and remediation report template.

modules.title: Guardrails, approvals and audit for configuration comparison
topics: Read-only credentials for all collectors; no write capability exposed to Claude through MCP
Opening a ServiceNow change record with the Table API and attaching the report; Flow Designer approval routing to a named approver
Publishing each comparison as a GitHub pull request with the report, evidence and plan for review
Audit log of prompts, tool calls, model outputs and human decisions, retained alongside the raw evidence
modules.lab: Wire the pipeline to create a ServiceNow change via the Table API and a GitHub pull request, then attempt an unapproved remediation and confirm it is blocked and logged.
modules.deliverable: Approval and audit workflow with blocked-action evidence.

modules.title: Scheduling, Terraform plan checks and GitHub Actions
topics: Running the comparison on a schedule in GitHub Actions and on pull requests that change Terraform code
Comparing terraform plan output against live collected state before apply; flagging drift on both sides
Notifications and report publishing: PR comments, ServiceNow updates, archived reports
Operating the pipeline: failures, retries, fixture refresh and runbook
modules.lab: Build the GitHub Actions workflow that runs the comparison, compares a Terraform plan against the live cloud load balancer, and comments the result on the pull request.
modules.deliverable: Scheduled comparison pipeline with Terraform drift check and runbook.

modules.title: Capstone: end-to-end physical-to-cloud comparison
topics: Collect, normalise, plan, diff and explain a physical F5 to cloud NetScaler migration end to end
Produce the approval package: plan, severity report, Claude explanation, evidence, ServiceNow change, pull request
Demo and acceptance review against the module one checklist
modules.lab: Run the full pipeline on the lab physical F5 and cloud NetScaler, produce the approval package with ServiceNow change and pull request, and present it for acceptance review against the module one checklist.
modules.deliverable: Complete comparison pipeline and approval package.

capstone: A repeatable pipeline that collects configuration from two platforms, normalises both into a canonical model, has Claude draft the migration plan and explain a deterministic diff, and delivers an approval package through a GitHub pull request and a ServiceNow change record with a full audit trail and no change applied without approval.

narration: hook

A data centre load balancer is moving to the cloud. The cut-over is on Saturday. The configuration on the new platform was rebuilt by hand from a spreadsheet, and nobody can say with certainty that the two sides match.
hook

What if Claude read both sides, object by object, told you exactly what differs, why it matters, and what to fix before the change window opens? That is configuration comparison, automated with Claude, and governed by people.
intro
Gennoor Tech presents Configuration Comparison Automation with Claude.
story

Two platforms. One verified difference report. Cloud to cloud, physical to cloud, or cloud back to physical, the problem is always the same: two configurations written in different dialects that must mean the same thing. You build the pipeline in ten modules. Claude plans, drafts and explains. Deterministic Python collects and diffs. A person approves every consequential action. And everything is logged.
path0

You start with the planning discipline: what a migration comparison must prove, which objects matter, and why a raw text diff between an F five and a NetScaler is worthless. Then you set up the workbench. Claude Code for interactive work, the Claude Agent S D K for the pipeline, and M C P servers that expose read-only collectors as tools Claude can call but never bypass.
path0

Day one ends with collection and normalisation. You pull running configuration from F five through iControl R E S T and t m s h, from Citrix NetScaler through the N I T R O A P I, from Radware Alteon, from other load balancers such as Anaya L B, and from Cisco A P I C and Terraform state. Every virtual server, pool, monitor, certificate and policy lands in one canonical Pydantic model, with provenance on every field and unknowns marked explicitly instead of guessed.
path1

On day two Claude plans. Given the source inventory and the target platform, it drafts the migration plan as structured J S O N: object mappings, feature gaps, dependency order and risks. It must cite the inventory it was given, and it must say plainly what cannot be mapped. Each plan step carries a confidence and an owner, so the review meeting argues about facts, not formatting. You test it with incomplete and contradictory input and watch it refuse to invent a mapping.
path2

Then the diff engine. Deterministic code compares canonical models field by field, classifies each difference by severity, and produces a machine-readable report. Claude never computes the diff. It reads the diff through tool use and writes the explanation, the drift summary and the remediation steps an engineer can act on, with every claim tied to a report line. You will seed a hidden persistence mismatch and watch the engine find it.
path3

Day three is governance. Collectors run with read-only credentials. Every report becomes a GitHub pull request with the evidence attached, and a ServiceNow change record created through the Table A P I and routed for approval in Flow Designer. Nothing is applied to any platform without a named approver, and the approval itself is part of the audit record.
path3

You then wire it into GitHub Actions: Terraform plan output compared against live state before apply, scheduled drift checks between platforms, and an audit trail that records every prompt, every tool call and every decision, so a reviewer can replay the run months later.
labs

Every lab runs against lab devices and recorded A P I responses, so you can break things safely. You will compare a physical F five with a cloud NetScaler, seed a hidden persistence timeout mismatch into the target, and prove the diff engine catches it, Claude explains it, and the tests never let it slip through. Then you attempt an unapproved remediation and prove the pipeline blocks it and logs the attempt.
stats
Three migration directions. Five platform A P I families. One canonical schema for every object. And zero changes applied without approval.
who

This course is for enterprise I T and network operations teams, load balancer and cloud migration engineers, and automation leads, in India and worldwide. You need basic networking, Python and command line skills. Prior use of Claude is helpful, not required.
cta
